sections.h2: What should a Michigan home seller know about the state first?
sections.html:
Michigan is a state of homeowners. The Census Bureau's QuickFacts table shows an owner-occupied housing rate of 73.2% for 2020 to 2024, a median owner-occupied home value of $231,600, and a median gross rent of $1,129. It counts 4,076,369 households and a July 2025 population estimate of 10,127,884.

The state has two peninsulas, the more populated Lower Peninsula and the heavily forested Upper Peninsula, joined across the Straits of Mackinac. Lansing is the capital, Detroit is the most populous city, and Wayne is the largest county. Michigan borders four of the five Great Lakes and has the longest freshwater coastline of any U.S. political subdivision, 3,288 miles, per Wikipedia. Water, snow, and age of housing stock all shape what a buyer finds during an inspection.

For a seller, the practical result is that the same statute works differently by place. The sections below cover the rules that apply in every Michigan county, and the guides by city and county on this site add the local office details.

sections.h2: Which local offices handle what in Michigan?
sections.html:
Michigan has 83 counties. Townships are divisions of counties, and cities, villages, and state universities hold home rule powers of differing degrees. A house sale touches several offices at once, and the tasks split roughly as follows.

  • City or township assessor: receives the principal residence exemption affidavit and rescission form, and decides whether a transfer uncaps taxable value.
  • County treasurer: collects the state real estate transfer tax on a recorded sale.
  • County register of deeds: records the deed, receives redemption payments after a foreclosure sale, and notifies the local tax collecting unit of a recorded transfer (MCL 211.7cc(17)).
  • District court: hears landlord-tenant summary proceedings.
  • Probate court: handles estates, and the small estate affidavit form PC 598 is available only where no real property is in the estate.

Treasury's property tax page groups the state's programs into categories that include deferment, forfeiture and foreclosure, exemptions, the Homestead Property Tax Credit, veterans and military personnel, and changes in ownership. A seller facing delinquent tax should start there and then call the county treasurer.

sections.h2: How long does a Michigan homeowner have to redeem after a foreclosure sale?
sections.html:
It depends on the property type and the mortgage balance. MCL 600.3240 sets these periods for foreclosure by advertisement.

  • Commercial, industrial, or multifamily property above 4 units: 6 months from the sale date.
  • Residential property of up to 4 units, where the amount claimed at the notice date is more than 66-2/3% of the original debt: 6 months.
  • Residential property of up to 4 units that is abandoned under the statute's test: 1 month, or 30 days under a separate abandonment section.
  • Agricultural property: 1 year, with a presumption tied to a filed federal Schedule F and a recorded affidavit.
  • Anything else: 1 year.

To redeem, the owner or a person with a recorded interest pays the sale bid, interest from the sale date at the mortgage rate, the sheriff's fee the purchaser paid, and a $5 custody fee if paid to the register of deeds. The purchaser records an affidavit stating the exact amount. A register of deeds in a county with a population between 750,000 and 1,500,000 will compute the figure on request for no more than $50.

sections.h2: What does a seller owe at closing in Michigan?
sections.html:
The statute puts the state real estate transfer tax on the seller or grantor, payable to the county treasurer where the property sits within 15 days after the deed is delivered (MCL 207.523). It applies to deeds and instruments of conveyance for consideration, and also to sale contracts and to transfers of a controlling interest in an entity that mostly holds real estate. If a seller later believes an exemption applied, the statute allows a refund request to Treasury. Ask the county treasurer or your closing agent for the current rate and the exemptions that fit your sale.

On the property tax side, a sale is a transfer of ownership that normally uncaps taxable value for the buyer in the following calendar year, with a list of exempt transfers in MCL 211.27a(7), according to Treasury. The seller's own filing is the rescission of the principal residence exemption, which the closing agent is supposed to supply forms for.

sections.h2: What are the main routes to selling a house in Michigan?
sections.html:
Most Michigan sales fall into a handful of situations, and each has its own paperwork. A seller who inherited a house works with the probate court because the small estate affidavit cannot cover real property. A seller behind on a mortgage works against the redemption clock described above. A seller with a tenant works within the summary proceedings schedule, and a security deposit must be passed to the buyer with notice to the tenant (MCL 554.614).

A seller who owns through a lady bird deed, trust, or land contract needs to read the ownership rules for the principal residence exemption, since Treasury lists who counts as an owner. Michigan Treasury also publishes information on tax forfeiture, foreclosure, and auction for owners who let property taxes go unpaid.

  • Inherited house: contact the probate court for the county where the decedent lived.
  • Behind on the mortgage: find the sale date and the redemption deadline on the certificate of sale.
  • Rented house: serve the right notice and keep the deposit paperwork.
  • Delinquent taxes: ask the county treasurer for the payoff and any deferment options.

sections.h2: How should I use the city and county guides on this site?
sections.html: Start with the guide for the county where the house sits, then add the city or township page if one exists. County offices differ in hours, fees, and recording steps, and the statutes above set only the outer rules. Each local guide covers what that office handles, and the statewide pages on property tax, probate, foreclosure, the principal residence exemption, eviction, and lady bird deeds fill in the rest.

faqs.q: How many counties does Michigan have?
faqs.a: Michigan has 83 counties. Townships are administrative divisions of a county, and cities, villages, and state universities hold home rule powers to varying degrees, according to the state's general description.

faqs.q: Who pays the transfer tax when a house is sold in Michigan?
faqs.a: The seller or grantor is liable under MCL 207.523, and the tax goes to the county treasurer within 15 days after the deed is delivered. A buyer who pays it for the seller can request a refund if an exemption applied.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Michigan?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau puts the median value of owner-occupied housing units in Michigan at $231,600 for 2020 to 2024. The QuickFacts page also lists a 73.2% owner-occupied housing rate for the same period.

faqs.q: Can I use the small estate affidavit to sell an inherited house?
faqs.a: No. Court form PC 598 requires that no real property be included in the decedent's estate, so a house needs a court proceeding with a personal representative.

faqs.q: How long can a lender wait before a foreclosure sale is final?
faqs.a: The redemption period after the sale is commonly 6 months for a residential mortgage over 66-2/3% of the original debt, and 1 year for property that fits none of the shorter categories, under MCL 600.3240.
